newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RBA says millenium bug could cost A$350 million.
newsitem.headline: RBA says millenium bug could cost A$350 million.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) said Australia's four major local banks could spend more than A$350 million to fix the computer problems posed by the Year 2000 millenium bug.
RBA deputy governor Graeme Thompson said the central bank was seeking assurances that local banks were making determined efforts to overcome the bug problem.
"The upshot for Australian banks is the need to spend big sums on replacing or reprogramming their data-dependent computer systems," he said in a speech to a business luncheon.
"For the four majors alone, the total cost could well be over A$350 million."
Thompson said the central bank, like the U.S. Fed, recognised the urgency of the millenium computer bug problem.

The Millennium bug is a world-wide programming problem that will cause many computers to view the year 2000 as the year 1900. The bug will occur as a result of a programming fault which only allows computers to accept the last two digits of a year.
As a result, companies will have to re-programme their computers to accept a four-digit field before 2000 in order to avoid computer chaos.
Thompson said the RBA was currently seeking assurance that Australian banks were giving the Year 2000 problem the high priority it warranted.

"We recently sent them a questionnaire asking each about progress in identifying the size of the problem for its operations, in drawing up a management programme to fix it and in assigning the necessary resources," he said.
"They should also be finding out what their major customers are doing about it," Thompson said.
Two of Australia's major banks said last month that fixing the millennium bug would represent a significant cost.

National Australia Bank Ltd, the nation's largest and most profitable bank, said a fairly significant investment would be needed to overcome the problem but it also represents an opportunity to standardise its worldwide network.
Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd, which is based in Melbourne along with NAB, said the bug problem will lead to a "measurable" but not large cost.
The other two major banks are based in Sydney. They are the Commonwealth Bank of Australia and Westpac Banking Corp . Each has assets of more than A$100 billion.
"Fixing the Year 2000 problem is not a glamorous task -- but it is no less important for that," Thompson said.
He said the Fed has recommended that financial institutions have new systems in place by the end of 1998 to allow time for thorough testing before January 2000.

"This will be needed because, in changing a lot of banking software, new bugs could be introduced along the way. More aggressive targets have been set for large banks where computer problems could do broad damage to the working of the financial system," Thompson said.
